citation: Haeussler, C., Harhoff, D., & Mueller, E. (2014). How patenting informs VC investors – The case of biotechnology. Research Policy, 43(8), 1286–1298. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.respol.2014.03.012
key_finding: The study uses Cox hazard models of time to first VC financing for 190 VC-seeking German and UK biotech firms (3,001 firm-quarters, 87 VC events). A larger stock of EPO patent applications speeds up first VC financing: the hazard ratio is 1.454 per unit of ln(1+stock), p<0.01, in the base model, and 1.56–1.63 in the full models. The share of applications already granted is positive but not significant (HR 1.115). Later patent-office information also matters: favourable news, meaning citations by large followers and oppositions, raises the hazard, while unfavourable news (X/Y search references, late search reports) lowers it.
quote: Consistent with H1, which is our base hypothesis, the application stock has a positive significant effect on the hazard. Thus, once companies apply for patent protection, they receive VC financing faster.
quote_version: Published journal version (Research Policy 43(8), Elsevier typeset PDF), read from the copy on the first author's University of Passau page. The abstract on p. 1286 says the same: "We find that the filing of patent applications is positively related to VC financing."
claim_note: The direction is right. Filed applications, not grants, are what predict faster first VC financing; grant share is not significant (H4 not supported), so the 'not only granted' part holds. Limits on using this for our metric: (1) the evidence covers only biotech in Germany and the UK, firms founded after 1990 that wanted VC, and observations up to Q2 2005. (2) It counts EPO applications only, logged as ln(1+cumulative stock) per quarter, not a binary has_patent_application flag. (3) The design is observational hazard modelling, so it does not show causation, and the sample is survivors only. A footnote reports a robustness check that includes failed German firms. (4) In the 98-firm subsample of patenting firms with search reports (Table 3, cols 5–6), the stock effect is about 1.42 and not significant. So within patenters, more applications add little. The signal mostly separates firms that file from firms that don't. (5) The paper's main point is that information produced later in examination also moves VC timing, beyond the filing itself.
metric_definition_in_paper: Outcome: time to first VC financing, measured quarterly and right-censored at the 2006 survey. The last period observed is Q2 2005. Key regressor: 'ln EPO application stock', the time-varying cumulative number of EPO patent applications as observable each quarter, plus 1 and logged. Other time-varying patent-office variables: share of applications with many X/Y search references, separate/belated search reports, share granted (EPO B1), share highly cited, cited by a large technology follower, and share opposed. These are aggregated into positive news and negative news. Controls: technological capabilities, high-risk startup, CEO industry experience, early-stage financings in the market, and dummies for spin-out type, therapeutics, founding period and country. Cox proportional hazards, Breslow ties. EPO applications are published 18 months after priority. The paper assumes VCs see the full application at filing, but it does not state explicitly whether the stock is timed by filing date or by publication date.
licence: Publisher copyright (© 2014 Elsevier B.V., all rights reserved); author-hosted copy, no open-access licence. PDF not saved to the repo.

citation: Farre-Mensa, Joan, Deepak Hegde, and Alexander Ljungqvist (2020). "What Is a Patent Worth? Evidence from the U.S. Patent 'Lottery'." Journal of Finance 75(2), 639-682. DOI: 10.1111/jofi.12867. (Also NBER Working Paper No. 23268, March 2017, revised December 2018.)
key_finding: The study uses examiner leniency as a quasi-random instrument for whether a startup's first patent application is approved. Approval raises the chance of raising VC funding by 1.7 pp within 1 year (p=0.053) and by 3.0 pp within 3 years (p<0.01), which is about 47% above the 6.4% baseline. It rises to 3.6 pp within 5 years. The effect is largest for follow-on rounds, inexperienced founders, non-hub states and IT firms. It is not significant in biochemistry or for second patent grants.
quote: Approval of a firm’s first patent application causes a startup’s chances of obtaining VC funding in the following year to increase by 1.7 percentage points (p=0.053 in column 1). Extending the window increases the effect to 2.7, 3.0, 3.4, and 3.6 percentage points over two, three, four, and five years, respectively (p<0.01).
quote_version: NBER Working Paper 23268, revised December 2018 (w23268.pdf). The published Journal of Finance version was paywalled (HTTP 403) and was not read, so its page numbers may differ.
claim_note: The claim is correct as stated. Approval of the first application causally raises the later probability of raising VC funding (2SLS, Table 7). There are four caveats. (1) The signal in the paper is approval of an application, not filing one. Every firm in the sample has applied, so the paper gives no direct support for has_patent_application (applied vs. did not apply) as a predictor. It only supports a granted first patent. (2) The effect is small in absolute terms: +3.0 pp on a 6.4% base over 3 years. For firms with no prior VC, the effect on raising a first round is only +1.3 pp (p=0.08). (3) The effect varies by firm type. It is concentrated in follow-on rounds, inexperienced founders, non-hub states and IT, and is not significant in biochemistry. (4) The sample is US small-entity first-time applicants from 2001 to 2009, with VC events taken from VentureXpert.
metric_definition_in_paper: The sample has 34,215 US first-time patent applicants. They are stand-alone, for-profit, small-entity firms with no applications in the prior 25 years, which first filed on or after 1 Jan 2001. Each got a first-action decision by 2009 and a final decision by 2013. The treatment is an indicator that the first patent application is approved. It is instrumented by the examiner's past approval rate, with art-unit-by-year and HQ-state fixed effects, controlling for log(1 + prior VC rounds). The outcome is an indicator that the startup raises VC funding (from VentureXpert) within 1 to 5 years after the first-action date. The median lag to the VC round is about 9 to 10 months.
licence: NBER working paper, copyright 2017 by the authors, all rights reserved (short quotations allowed with credit). This is not an open licence, so no PDF was saved to papers/pdf/.

citation: Block, J. H., De Vries, G., Schumann, J. H., & Sandner, P. (2014). Trademarks and venture capital valuation. Journal of Business Venturing, 29(4), 525-542. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jbusvent.2013.07.006 (earlier SSRN WP 2064508, 'Trademarks and Venture Capital Funding', 2012; also Chapter 4 of G. de Vries, 'Venture Capital: Relations with the Economy and Intellectual Property', PhD thesis, Erasmus University Rotterdam, 2013, Tinbergen Institute Research Series no. 569)
key_finding: The sample is 4,816 VC funding rounds of 2,341 US VC-backed start-ups, 1998-2007. Start-ups that had filed at least one US trademark application before a funding round had about 24.7% higher post-money valuations (log coefficient 0.247, p<0.01). Each extra trademark application added about 1.6%, with diminishing returns (negative squared term). The journal abstract calls this an inverted U for both the number and the breadth of trademarks. The trademark effect is smaller in later rounds once the start-up has moved to a more advanced development stage.
quote: In Model 2, we introduce the trademark dummy variable. An increased valuation of 24.7% is estimated for start-ups that applied for at least one trademark (p < 0.01).
quote_page: 84 (printed page of the thesis; PDF page 97). Results are in Table 4.4, printed page 83.
quote_version: Thesis-chapter version: Chapter 4, 'Trademarks and venture capital valuation' ('Based on Block et al. (2013)'), in G. de Vries' 2013 Erasmus PhD thesis, read from the Erasmus repository PDF. The JBV journal version could not be read: ScienceDirect returned 403 and SSRN returned 403. Its coefficients and page numbers may differ.
claim_note: The paper supports a positive link between trademarks and VC valuation (post-money valuation in VentureXpert). It does not test whether trademarks predict receiving VC investment at all, because every firm in the sample is already VC-backed (selected on first round being seed/early). So 'associated with VC investment' goes beyond the evidence. The measure is US trademark applications filed before the round date, not registrations. The effect of the trademark count is non-linear (positive but diminishing; the journal abstract says inverted U) and weaker at later development stages. The authors call the results associations or signals, and they check endogeneity only by re-running on first rounds. Evidence is US-only, 1998-2007.
metric_definition_in_paper: Unit: one VC funding round (VentureXpert, US, 1998-2007; firms whose first round was seed or early stage). Dependent variable: log post-money valuation. Trademark data: USPTO trademark applications, hand-matched by company name and former aliases. 'Trademark dummy' = 1 if the start-up filed at least one US trademark application before the funding date; filings after the funding date are excluded. 'Trademark applications' = cumulative count, also used squared. 'Trademark breadth' = number of distinct Nice classes. Controls: patent applications (PATSTAT), round, syndicate size, MSCI index, year, investor type, VC age and experience, start-up age, development stage, industry and region. Estimation: OLS with errors clustered by firm, plus firm fixed effects in some models. 58.9% of rounds had a trademark.

citation: Catalini, C., Guzman, J., & Stern, S. (2019). Hidden in Plain Sight: Venture Growth with or without Venture Capital. NBER Working Paper No. 26521, National Bureau of Economic Research, December 2019. DOI: 10.3386/w26521. (JEL G24, L26. No journal version found; an earlier draft dated Oct 2017 also circulates.)
licence: NBER working paper, (c) 2019 the authors, all rights reserved (short excerpts may be quoted with credit). Not an open licence, so no PDF was saved.
key_finding: The paper uses logit models on about 13.2M US business registrations (1995-2005). It controls for corporate form, name, Delaware incorporation, patent and industry. With those controls, a trademark application within a year of founding is linked to about 2.0x higher odds of raising VC (Table 3 col 3, IRR 2.024). Among firms that never raised VC, it is linked to about 6.0x higher odds of an IPO or acquisition within 10 years (Table 5 col 4, IRR 6.030). Patents predict much more strongly: about 38.8x for a patent alone and 141x for a patent plus Delaware incorporation.
quote: Firms with intellectual property are also more likely to raise VC. Firms with a trademark are 102% more likely to raise VC, and firms with a patent are 38 times more likely to receive VC financing.
claim_note: Supported, with some limits. Early trademark and patent filings do predict both VC funding and equity growth (IPO or acquisition). The paper says this is predictive, not causal: these are founding "digital signatures" of quality (fn 3, p.4). (1) Trademark is a weak predictor of VC, at about 2x, next to patent (39x) or patent plus Delaware (141x). (2) Trademark matters MORE for growth without VC than for VC. Page 6 says: "With the exception of trademark, which is more salient among non-venture-backed firms". Page 20 says an early trademark is "an indicator that the firm is planning to commercialize a product or service" and fits with bootstrapping through sales. (3) The signal is rare: 0.08% of firms have one. (4) Small internal inconsistency: the text on p.16 says trademark firms are "3 times" more likely in col 2, but Table 3 shows 4.291. (5) Related Guzman and Stern work also uses trademark as a quality input (Science 2015; NBER 'Nowcasting and Placecasting' 2017; AEJ:Policy 2020), but I did not read or verify those papers here. Our has_trademark is a valid proxy only if it is measured within about 1 year of founding and before the funding or outcome date.
metric_definition_in_paper: Data: Startup Cartography Project business registrations in 49 US states plus DC, 1995-2005, 13,231,305 firms. "Trademark" = 1 if the firm applies for USPTO trademark protection within a year of registration (p.15; mean 0.0008). "Patent" = 1 if the firm holds a patent application filed by it, or assigned to it, within its first year (mean 0.002). Outcomes: "Gets Venture Capital", from VC deals matched to Thomson Reuters VentureXpert (0.08% of firms; "Gets VC in 2 Years" is used later); "Equity growth" = IPO (SDC) or acquisition within 10 years of founding (0.13%). Models are logits reporting incidence rate ratios, fitted on a random 50% training sample, with standard errors clustered by state-year. The controls are corporation, short name, eponymous name, Delaware incorporation, patent-by-Delaware interactions and name-based industry dummies.

citation: Howell, Sabrina T. (2017). "Financing Innovation: Evidence from R&D Grants." American Economic Review 107(4): 1136-1164. DOI: 10.1257/aer.20150808. (Working-paper versions: "Financing Constraints as Barriers to Innovation: Evidence from R&D Grants to Energy Startups", job market paper, Oct 14 2014 / Jan 7 2015; SSRN 2687457.)
licence: Author-hosted working paper (Jan 7, 2015 job market paper), no open licence stated (author copyright); published AER version is AEA copyright
key_finding: The study uses a sharp regression discontinuity on ranked applicants to DOE SBIR (EERE and Fossil Energy offices). Winning a roughly $150k Phase 1 grant raises the chance of later VC by about 9 percentage points, from about 10% to 19%. Estimates range from 7.2 to 14 pp across bandwidths, and the effect within two years of the grant is 7 pp. The effect is stronger for younger and more financially constrained firms. The larger Phase 2 grant has no effect on VC.
quote: I show that a Phase 1 grant of $150,000 approximately doubles a firm's chance of subsequently receiving venture capital (VC) investment, increasing the long term probability by 9 percentage points from 10% to 19%. Within two years of the grant, the effect is 7 percentage points.
quote_version: Working paper: "Financing Constraints as Barriers to Innovation: Evidence from R&D Grants to Energy Startups", job market paper dated January 7, 2015 (Yale-hosted PDF). This is not the published AER text.
claim_note: The claim is substantially correct. The published AER abstract (read via the EconPapers metadata, not the article PDF) says "An early-stage award approximately doubles the probability that a firm receives subsequent venture capital". In the Jan 2015 working paper the effect is +9 pp, from 10% to 19%; the 9.8 pp estimate is significant at the 1% level. Caveats for has_public_rd_grant: (1) It is a local causal effect of narrowly winning versus narrowly losing among DOE energy/cleantech SBIR applicants, not a correlation across the whole startup population. (2) It covers Phase 1 only; Phase 2 shows no VC effect. (3) The effect is concentrated in young, financially constrained firms and varies by period: 7 pp in 2005-09, 19 pp in 2009-13. (4) VC is "ever received after the grant", matched from ThomsonOne, Preqin, Cleantech i3, CrunchBase and CapitalIQ. The exact figures in the published version could not be checked.
metric_definition_in_paper: Treatment is winning a DOE SBIR Phase 1 grant (about $150k) in the EERE or Fossil Energy offices. Identification is a sharp regression discontinuity on DOE officials' within-competition applicant ranks, centred at the award cutoff, using competitions from 1995 onward. The outcome VC^Post equals 1 if the firm ever received VC after its first grant. VC deals were matched by firm name and state from ThomsonOne, Preqin, Cleantech Group i3, CrunchBase and CapitalIQ, then hand-checked. A two-year horizon is also reported.

citation: Santoleri, P., Mina, A., Di Minin, A., & Martelli, I. (2024). The Causal Effects of R&D Grants: Evidence from a Regression Discontinuity. Review of Economics and Statistics, 106(6), 1495-1510. https://doi.org/10.1162/rest_a_01233 (earlier version: LEM Working Paper 2020/18, Scuola Superiore Sant'Anna)
key_finding: The paper uses a sharp RDD on SME Instrument Phase II competitions from 2014 to 2017. The running variable is the evaluation rank relative to the cutoff where the budget runs out. Winning raises the probability of later private equity by about 7 to 11.7 percentage points on a 4% mean, which is up to a threefold increase. It also raises the equity amount by 46-97% and the number of deals by about 8-17%. The authors trace the effect to the funding itself, not to certification: losers who received only the "Seal of Excellence" quality stamp did not improve.
quote: More precisely, estimates indicate that winning the grant increases the probability of receiving external equity by about 7 and 11.7 percentage points, relative to a 4% mean. Hence, the receipt of R&D grants triggers up to a threefold increase in the likelihood of receiving follow-on equity investments.
quote_page: 19 (page number printed in the Just Accepted manuscript; also PDF page 19)
quote_version: MIT Press "Review of Economics and Statistics Just Accepted MS" rest_a_01233, dated 14 July 2022, as posted on IRIS Sant'Anna. I could not get the final typeset version (pages 1495-1510, paywalled). The 2020 LEM WP 2020/18, which I also read, has the same finding in an earlier form (Table 5).
claim_note: The claim is supported, with caveats. (1) The paper studies Phase II grants only, averaging about EUR 1.6M. The 2020 working paper finds that Phase I grants (EUR 50k) do not affect firm performance. (2) The outcome is "private equity" from BvD Zephyr, which covers private financing deals generally. It is not a VC-specific measure. (3) The estimate is local: it compares winners with near-miss losers, all of whom passed the quality threshold. It is not a comparison of grantees with the general SME population. (4) The horizon is short, with outcomes measured as of March 2019. (5) The losing firms that received the Seal of Excellence certificate saw no benefit, so a simple 'applied/certified' flag would not carry the effect. For has_public_rd_grant this backs a positive signal for large EU R&D grants (SME Instrument Phase II, or EIC Accelerator-type), not for small grants.
licence: Publisher copyright (MIT Press / President and Fellows of Harvard College and MIT). IRIS shows the file as open access under "Copyright dell'editore". The LEM working paper has no stated open licence. I did not save the PDF.
metric_definition_in_paper: Treatment is winning an SME Instrument Phase II grant in a 2014-2017 EASME competition. The design is a sharp RD on the centred evaluation rank around the cutoff where the budget runs out, using infinite, ±10 and ±5 rank bandwidths. Applicants are linked to ORBIS. The equity outcome is a dummy for having received private equity investment after the competition, as of March 2019, from ORBIS Zephyr private-financing data covering 1997-2019. Secondary outcomes are log(1+amount) and log(1+number of deals). Pre-period mean of the dummy is 0.04.

citation: Conti, A., Peukert, C., & Roche, M. (2025). Beefing IT Up for Your Investor? Engagement with Open Source Communities, Innovation, and Startup Funding: Evidence from GitHub. Organization Science, 36(4), 1551-1573. https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.2023.18348
key_finding: The authors compare startups that engage with external GitHub repositories against matched control startups using a difference-in-differences linear probability model. After engagement starts, the probability of having raised a first round by quarter t rises by 15 percentage points with the fewest controls (+65% over the mean) and by 8 pp with the full set of fixed effects (Table 6 col. 4, +36% over the mean of about 0.22). The effect is larger for startups that engage before their first round, is about 9 pp larger for external than for internal-only repository activity, and is strongest for novel-technology and AI/Blockchain startups. Event-study pre-trends are flat.
quote: Our results suggest that engaging with OSCs on GitHub is associated with an increase in the likelihood of receiving funding by at least 36%.
quote_page: 1552 (printed journal page; PDF page 3 of the IE-repository download, which adds a cover page)
quote_version: Published journal version, Organization Science 36(4), July-August 2025 (INFORMS PDF, CC BY 4.0), downloaded from the IE University repository
claim_note: (1) 160,065 is correct, but it counts only the U.S. Crunchbase startups founded 2005-2020 (p.1556). The GitHub link covers 14,881 of them, the regression sample is a matched 34,298 (7,207 engaged plus 27,091 controls, Table 5), and Product Hunt is used only for the product-launch outcome. (2) "At least 36%" is correct, but it is not an odds figure. It is a linear-probability DiD coefficient of 0.081 on 'has raised a first round by quarter t', divided by a mean of about 0.22 (Table 6 col. 4, p.1561). It is an association, not a causal effect. (3) "GitHub activity accelerates in the 12 months before the first round" is overstated. Online Appendix Table A14 (described on p.1566) fits a linear trend over the 12 months before and after the first round, with a separate intercept at the round. It finds a rising pre-round trend in making a repository public, and in making repos public that are later forked. However, it finds 'no significant change in the trend after receiving financing', and the slope for forked repos stays the same afterwards. This is a steady increase, not an acceleration, and it covers only repository publishing, not GitHub activity in general. The only other timing facts are these: 80% of funded engaged startups engage before funding, and on average they start GitHub activity 5 months before the first round (p.1559). There is also a quarterly event study, 4 quarters before to 8 after the start of engagement, with flat pre-trends (Fig. 3, p.1562). DEFINITION of external engagement: EngagementWithOSC_i = 1 if the startup's GitHub ORGANIZATION account makes at least one public event on an external repository during the observed period (p.1559). An external repository is one created and controlled by another organization, which the focal org can change only through pull requests, issues, or forking (fn 4). Internal repos are those the firm created and holds. Private repos are excluded. Data come from GH Archive public events since Feb 2011, linked to Crunchbase through the website listed on the org account (p.1557). Of external events, 96% are forks, 2% watch (star) events and 1% push events (p.1557). The ML use-case classification covers commits, pull requests and forks. PostGitHub_gt switches on in the quarter the first external event occurs, the outcome is censored at 2020q2, and each startup is followed for up to 24 quarters. TEAM: there is no team-based engagement measure. Founders' or employees' personal accounts are not used; only organization accounts are. 'Top Team' is a matching and control variable equal to 1 if a founder or CXO (CEO, CTO, CFO or CMO) is in Crunchbase's top 1,000 people (fn 15-16). Controls are up to 5 startups from the same state and founding year, in the same software-share bin, with the same Top Team value, that have no GitHub org or only internal-repo activity. A readme-only activity test shows that cosmetic activity is not linked to funding (Table 11).
metric_definition_in_paper: Engagement is measured on the startup's GitHub organization account, not on personal accounts. The account is linked to Crunchbase through the website it lists. GH Archive public events on repositories the org does not control (forks 96%, watch/star 2%, push 1%) define EngagementWithOSC_i: at least one such event during the observed period. PostGitHub_gt = 1 from the quarter of the first external event, for the startup and its matched group. The outcome is whether the startup has raised a first round by quarter t (Crunchbase), quarterly, censored at 2020q2, with up to 24 quarters per startup. The model includes startup, group-by-quarter, industry-by-quarter and startup-by-age fixed effects. The pre-funding dynamics come from Table A14 (Online Appendix): a linear time trend over the 12 months before and after the first round, with an intercept shift at the round, for (1) making a new repo public, (2) making a private repo public, and (3) making a repo public that is later forked. The event study (Fig. 3) runs from 4 quarters before to 8 quarters after the first external engagement.

The Role of Open Source Software for Global Startups" (the title page inside reads "...The Strategic Role of..."). Harvard Business School Working Paper No. 24-040, first released January 2024 and revised August 2024; SSRN 4699182. It is not published; Nagle's CV dated 24 Sep 2025 lists it as "Under Review". COMPANION PAPER (a different study): Wright, N.L., Nagle, F., Greenstein, S. (2023). "Open source software and global entrepreneurship." Research Policy 52(9), article 104846, doi:10.1016/j.respol.2023.104846. The published version carries a CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 licence. The earlier draft is HBS Working Paper 20-139, June 2023 author's original on Harvard DASH. Both papers have three authors; there is no two-author "Wright & Nagle" paper.

Also read for the Research Policy paper: https://dash.harvard.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/41af0695-9b45-4336-bfc4-4a0f2e341b75/content (DASH author's original = HBS WP 20-139, June 2023)
key_finding: WP 24-040 is a firm-level study of 61,379 PitchBook software ventures founded 2000-2016, with GitHub data for 2017-2022. Cross-sectionally, a 1% rise in commits goes with about a 0.3% rise in funding and valuation (Table 2: log deal size 0.302, or 0.277 in the matched sample; log valuation 0.278, or 0.252 matched). With firm and year fixed effects, a one-year lag and a CEM-matched sample, the estimate falls to 0.03% for funding (0.026) and 0.1% for valuation (0.091). The effect on successful exit is about zero. The authors conclude that at least two-thirds of the cross-sectional link is selection. The Research Policy 2023 paper is a separate country-level study: a 1% rise in a country's GitHub commits goes with 0.2-0.4% more new IT ventures and 0.4-0.8% more venture financing value in the following year (OLS and 2SLS).
quote: Cross-sectionally, a 1 percent increase in GitHub participation—i.e., code contributions labeled as “commits”—is associated with a 0.3 percent increase in total funding and valuations. Once we incorporate fixed effects in a matched sample to help account for selection, these effects fall to a 0.03-0.1 percent increase in funding and valuations.
quote_page: Printed pages 4-5 (PDF pages 6-7). The supporting coefficients are in Tables 2-3 on printed page 37 (PDF page 39).
quote_version: HBS Working Paper 24-040, August 2024 revision (PDF created 5 Sep 2024; table header dated August 21, 2024)
claim_note: The 0.3% figure is real, but it is only the cross-sectional OLS estimate (with age, country and sub-industry fixed effects). That estimate mixes in selection: better firms are the ones that contribute to open source. The paper's preferred within-firm estimate is much smaller: 1% more commits in year t-1 goes with about 0.03% more funding and about 0.1% higher valuation in year t, and roughly zero effect on exit. The authors attribute at least two-thirds of the 0.3% to selection. The claim also names the wrong paper. The figure comes from WP 24-040, which has three authors (Wright, Nagle and Greenstein), not from a "Wright & Nagle" paper. It does not come from the Research Policy 2023 paper either, which works at the country level and measures new ventures and financing, not firm valuation. Finally, "participation" in the paper means the log level of commits, not a growth or acceleration rate.
metric_definition_in_paper: The unit is the firm-year. The main regressor is log(1 + GitHub commits) in year t-1, counting commits that the firm's employees made to open source projects. GitHub matched contributors to firms by the domain of their commit email addresses and handed over proprietary data, so this is not based on public organisation accounts; the authors say org accounts alone would undercount firm activity. A secondary regressor is a dummy for whether the firm contributed at all. Commits are also split by project type: internal (firm-owned), external new or old projects, and high or low firm share of a project's commits (threshold 50%, "new" meaning the project is at most 2 years old). Outcomes come from PitchBook: log yearly deal size (years without a deal set to 0), log post-money valuation (carried forward between rounds, available for about 35% of firms), and successful exit (IPO or acquisition). Specifications: a cross-section with age, country and sub-industry fixed effects, and a panel with firm and year fixed effects on a CEM-matched sample, with standard errors clustered by firm. Robustness checks include no lag, committer counts and a Bartik-style instrument. The Research Policy 2023 paper instead uses country-year GitHub commits for 2000-2016, with OLS and 2SLS, against Crunchbase/Preqin counts of ventures and financing. Neither paper measures acceleration (growth in commits). The within-firm fixed-effects estimate, which relates changes in a firm's lagged log commits to its outcomes, is the closest proxy.

citation: Hsu, David H. (2007). Experienced entrepreneurial founders, organizational capital, and venture capital funding. Research Policy, 36(5), 722-741. DOI: 10.1016/j.respol.2007.02.022
key_finding: The sample is 149 start-ups, and every one already had VC backing. Within it, more prior founding experience goes with a higher chance that the Series A VC was a direct personal contact of the founders: doubling the number of start-ups founded raises that chance by about 19% (5% level, p.735). It also goes with about 23% higher pre-money valuation (5% level, p.737). Among founders who had founded before, a prior start-up that returned an IRR of 100% or more adds about 29% to the direct-tie chance (only significant at 8%, p.736) and about a 39% valuation premium (5% level, p.738).
quote: First, prior founding experience (especially financially successful experience) increases both the likelihood of VC funding via a direct tie and venture valuation.
quote_page: 722 (printed page number; the abstract, PDF page 1)
quote_version: Published journal version (Elsevier typeset PDF, Research Policy 36(5), 722-741), as hosted on the author's Wharton faculty site
claim_note: The valuation half of the claim is supported. Prior founding experience goes with a higher Series A pre-money valuation: about +23% per doubling of prior start-ups (p.737), and the effect weakens in the specification with interaction terms (5-3). A financially successful prior start-up carries about a 39% premium (p.738). The half saying experience 'increases the likelihood of VC funding' is wrong as stated. Every firm in the sample had already completed a Series A VC round, so the paper never tests whether serial founders are more likely to get VC at all. What it tests is whether the funding came through a direct personal tie with the VC (Table 3: 0.54 vs 0.29 direct-contact rate, p.734). Other limits: the data are cross-sectional survey correlations, N=149, drawn from firms that applied to the MIT E-Lab program, funded in 1996-2000 with about 67% of them funded in 1999-2000, and 52% are Internet firms. For a serial_founder signal, this paper backs valuation and deal sourcing among firms that were funded. It does not back predicting which firms get funded.
metric_definition_in_paper: The source is a founder or executive survey of start-ups that applied to MIT's Entrepreneurship Lab (E-Lab) by 2000. To qualify, a firm had to have fewer than about 35 employees and to have completed a Series A VC round; 149 responded. The key regressor is 'Number of start-ups founded': a count of the start-ups the current founding team started before, with co-founders of the same earlier start-up counted once (mean 1.06; used as a log). A second variable is the 'High prior start-up return' dummy: 1 if a previous start-up of a team member liquidated at an IRR of 100% or more on its Series A investment (mean 0.30). There are two outcomes, both measured at the Series A round. The first is a dummy for whether the Series A investor was a direct personal contact of the founding team, estimated by probit. The second is log pre-money valuation, estimated by OLS on log-log data. Footnote 17 (p.735) reports that the results hold, and are often stronger, when a team's prior start-ups are counted only if they were VC-backed.

citation: Zhang, J. (2011). The advantage of experienced start-up founders in venture capital acquisition: evidence from serial entrepreneurs. Small Business Economics, 36(2), 187-208. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11187-009-9216-4 (online 18 June 2009). Earlier version: IZA Discussion Paper No. 2964, July 2007.
licence: IZA Discussion Paper, free to read from IZA. The PDF and IZA page show no open licence (no CC). The journal version is Springer copyright and paywalled.
key_finding: The early-stage advantage only shows up for founders whose earlier firm was itself VC-backed. Their later start-ups close the first VC round about 9.5 months sooner and raise about $4.1M more in it (1996 dollars; the average first round is $7.47M). Founders whose earlier firms were not VC-backed get no faster access and no larger first round. They do raise more once later rounds count: about $0.8M more per round and $1.61M more in total.
quote: I find that entrepreneurs with venture-backed founding experience gain access to VC more quickly and raise more VC in the first round than novice entrepreneurs. ... experienced entrepreneurs, also with prior founding experience but without connections to VC, do not have quicker access to VC and do not raise more VC in the first round than novice entrepreneurs.
quote_version: IZA Discussion Paper No. 2964 (July 2007), working-paper version. The published Small Business Economics version is paywalled and was not read, so its wording, page numbers and coefficients may differ.
metric_definition_in_paper: Data: VentureOne VC deals from 1992Q1 to 2001Q4 (22,479 rounds in 11,029 US firms). Founder biographies exist for only 5,972 firms (10,530 founders), and which firms have them is not random. Only firms that got VC are included, and firms founded before 1992 are dropped. Founder groups: (1) 'repeat entrepreneur', matched to two or more firms in VentureOne (304 people), so their later firms carry VC-backed prior experience; (2) 'experienced entrepreneur', one VentureOne firm but a biography that mentions earlier founding (2,563 people), treated as non-VC-backed experience; (3) 'novice', no prior founding (7,663 people). Each firm is assigned to its most experienced founder. Outcomes: months from founding to the close of the round labelled 'first round'; first-round amount; amount in any round; total VC raised. Amounts are in millions of 1996 dollars. Method: OLS with controls for start-year or closing-year, 16 industry dummies, high-tech-center dummies, round-class dummies and firm age.
claim_note: The claim is too broad. 'More and faster' at the early stage holds only for founders whose earlier firm was VC-backed, measured on their subsequent firms. Serial founders whose earlier firms were not VC-backed get VC no faster and raise no more in the first round. They raise only modestly more once later rounds are counted. Other limits: (a) the sample includes only firms that got VC, so the paper says nothing about the chance of getting VC at all (footnote 2); (b) founder data are incomplete and not randomly missing; (c) the results are correlations, and the author points out self-selection among repeat founders. For a serial_founder metric: a plain 'founded before' flag would overstate the early-round effect. Prior VC-backed founding is the signal that matters.

citation: Cao, Ruiqing (2019). "Information Frictions in New Venture Finance: Evidence from Product Hunt Rankings." Working paper, Department of Economics, Harvard University, draft dated June 22, 2019 (58 pp.). Unpublished; no DOI. The copy found is hosted by Cambridge Judge Business School.
key_finding: The paper uses two traction-weighted instruments (same-day BigTech launches and staff re-launches of earlier submissions) that push startups down the Product Hunt daily ranking. Each one-rank drop lowers the chance of a seed or Series A round within 6 months by about 0.23 pp, which is 9.5% of the 2.43% base rate (range 0.13-0.39 pp across specifications). The effect is concentrated in the top half of the daily feed (about 0.37-0.41 pp per rank, versus about 0.09 pp below the median). It is driven mainly by teams outside VC hubs and is larger for teams with at least one female maker.
quote: I estimate that each downward shift in rankings induced by the instruments leads to a decline in the probability of raising seed (including convertible note) and series A rounds by 0.23 percentage points within 6 months, or a 9.5% decline upon the average fundraising probability of 2.43%.
quote_version: Working paper draft dated June 22, 2019 (PDF created 2019-06-22), hosted at jbs.cam.ac.uk. No later or published version was found.
claim_note: The direction is right: an exogenously better daily rank raises later VC funding. Caveats for the backtest: (1) The outcome is narrow: a seed (including convertible note) or Series A round recorded in CrunchBase within 6 months, not VC funding in general. (2) The effect per rank is small in absolute terms (about 0.23 pp on a 2.43% base) and nonlinear, concentrated among products ranked at or above the daily median (median rank is 13). (3) The rank is imputed: it is the order of non-family/friend/bot upvotes at 11:59 PM PT on launch day, not the official rank, though the two correlate at Spearman 0.84. (4) The sample is featured tech launches from 2015Q2 to 2018Q1 by startups founded at most 5 years earlier that have not yet raised Series B (23,119 launches by 20,508 firms). (5) This is an unpublished working paper (June 2019 draft), not peer-reviewed. The 2020 date in our reference appears to be only the upload date of the hosted copy.
metric_definition_in_paper: ProductRank is the launch-day position among featured products. It is imputed by ordering non-family/friend/bot cumulative upvotes at 11:59 PM PT on launch day and enters the regressions as minus rank, so higher means better. Data come from the Product Hunt API, matched to CrunchBase by website domain. The outcome is a dummy for a seed (including convertible note) or Series A round within 6 months of launch. The rank is instrumented with TractionWeightedExternalLaunches, the sum of predicted traction from a regularized Poisson model, over same-day BigTech/large-company launches or re-launched past submissions. Controls are launch-hour, day-of-week and year-quarter fixed effects plus hunter, maker and post controls; standard errors are clustered by launch date.

citation: He, Hao; Yang, Haoqin; Burckhardt, Philipp; Kapravelos, Alexandros; Vasilescu, Bogdan; Kästner, Christian (2026). Six Million (Suspected) Fake Stars on GitHub: A Growing Spiral of Popularity Contests, Spam, and Malware. In 2026 IEEE/ACM 48th International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE '26), Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, April 12-18, 2026. ACM, 16 pp. DOI: 10.1145/3744916.3764531. Preprint arXiv:2412.13459 (v1, 18 Dec 2024, was titled "4.5 Million (Suspected) Fake Stars in GitHub: A Growing Spiral of Popularity Contests, Scams, and Malware"; v2, 6 Sep 2025, is the ICSE camera-ready text).
licence: CC-BY 4.0 (shown on the arXiv listing and on page 1 of the paper)
key_finding: The authors ran StarScout over GHArchive data from Jul 2019 to Dec 2024. It flagged 6.0M suspected fake stars across 26,254 repos. After postprocessing, 18,617 repos had fake-star campaigns, involving 301k accounts and 3.81M fake stars. Fake stars are a small share of all stars (<=1% per month) but surged in 2024: in July 2024, 16.66% of popular repos (3,499) had campaigns. Most fake stars promote short-lived phishing or malware repos. Fake stars bring real stars only in the short term (<2 months) and become a liability after that.
quote: In total, StarScout identified six million (suspected) fake stars across 26,254 repositories before the postprocessing step; among these stars, 1.06 million are identified with the low activity signature and 4.93 million with the lockstep signature. In the postprocessing step, StarScout identified 18,617 repositories with fake star campaigns and 301k participating accounts (corresponding to 3.81 million fake stars).
quote_page: 5 (printed page number; also PDF page 5). The headline pairing "6.0 million fake stars and 18,617 repositories with fake star campaigns" appears on printed page 2.
quote_version: arXiv v2 (2412.13459v2, 6 Sep 2025), formatted as the ICSE '26 paper
metric_definition_in_paper: Data source is GHArchive on BigQuery: WatchEvents (stars) from Jul 2019 to Dec 2024, processed in overlapping 6-month chunks. Two detectors. (1) Low-activity signature: an account whose only WatchEvent is a single star, plus at most one other event in the same repo on the same day. These count only in repos with >=50 such suspect stars. (2) Lockstep signature: CopyCatch with n=50, m=10, dt=30 days, rho=0.5, i.e. clusters of >=50 accounts and >=10 repos where each repo gets >=25 stars from those accounts within 30 days. Postprocessing aggregates stars by month. A repo counts as running a "fake star campaign" if some month has >50 fake stars making up >50% of that month's stars, and its all-time fake share is >10%. Accounts that starred during those spike months count as campaign accounts.
claim_note: The figures are right, but the claim mixes two stages of the pipeline. The paper's intro does say "6.0 million fake stars and 18,617 repositories with fake star campaigns". Section 3.3 shows these numbers do not describe the same set of repos. The 6.0M suspected stars come before postprocessing and are spread across 26,254 repos (1.06M low-activity plus 4.93M lockstep). The 18,617 campaign repos come after postprocessing and correspond to 3.81M fake stars from 301k accounts. So "~6M across ~18.6k repos" is wrong if read literally; use either 6.0M/26,254 or 3.81M/18,617. The title in the claim is from v1 (Dec 2024, data to Oct 2024), which reported different numbers: 4.53M stars across 22,915 repos before postprocessing, and 15,835 campaign repos with 3.1M stars from 278k accounts. The final title says "Spam", not "Scams".

citation: Runa Capital. "ROSS Index Methodology" (Runa Open Source Startup Index), web page, runacap.com/ross-index/methodology/ (accessed 2026-11-20; current text covers changes through Q1 2026). Also Runa Capital (2024), "ROSS Index: Annual report 2023", PDF slide report, 17 pp., created 2024-03-13, https://runacap.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/ROSS-Index-2023-Annual.pdf. Industry index by a VC firm, not peer reviewed, no DOI.
key_finding: ROSS is a methodology, not an empirical study, so it has no effect estimate. It looks at GitHub repos with 1,000+ stars and ranks them by how fast their star count grows relative to its starting size, not by stars added. It keeps only repos tied to startups (founded under 10 years ago, under $100M raised, not acquired or public), lists one repo per startup, and publishes the top 20 each quarter (top 50 in the annual report). From 2020 to 2023 the ranking used an annualized quarterly growth rate. Since Q1 2024 it uses the highest 90-day growth ratio, and since Q1 2026 repos that first reach 1,000 stars during the quarter can also qualify.
quote: In 2020-2023, we calculated the relative growth of stars within a fixed period (quarter or year) for all repos with at least 1,000 stars at the start of the period. For those rankings, we used the annualized growth rate calculated as AGR = (value now / value 1 quarter ago)⁴ – 1.
quote_page: No page number (HTML page); section "Old calculation approach". A matching passage is on printed page 3 of the 2023 Annual report PDF: "based on the annualised growth rate (AGR) of GitHub stars at their repositories within a period."
claim_note: The claim is right that ROSS ranks open-source startups by relative GitHub star growth. It is right about the annualized growth rate only for 2020–2023: AGR = (stars now / stars one quarter ago)^4 − 1, and the 2023 annual report also uses AGR. Since Q1 2024 the ranking uses the highest ratio (stars at end / stars at start) over any 90-day window ending in the quarter. This ratio is not annualized and the windows slide. Since Q1 2026 a repo only needs 1,000+ stars by the end of the quarter. A repo that crosses 1,000 during the quarter is scored as stars at quarter end ÷ 1,000. Earlier versions required 1,000+ stars at the start of the period. For ranking within one quarter, AGR and the plain quarterly ratio give the same order, because AGR is the ratio to the fourth power minus 1. The claim also leaves out several rules: the 1,000-star minimum, the startup filter (under 10 years old, under $100M raised, product tied to the repo, not acquired or public), keeping only the best repo per startup, and publishing only the top 20 or 50. For our star_growth baseline, the threshold and the relative-growth definition matter more than whether the rate is annualized.
licence: Publisher copyright (Runa Capital website and PDF). No open-access licence, so the PDF was not saved to papers/pdf/.
metric_definition_in_paper: Data: public GitHub star counts (startup details from Crunchbase, media and other public sources). Who is eligible: repos with 1,000+ stars at the start of the period (2020 to Q4 2025), or by the end of the quarter (since Q1 2026). Score for 2020–2023: AGR = (stars now / stars one quarter ago)^4 − 1, measured over a fixed quarter or year. Score since Q1 2024: the highest ratio of stars at end to stars at start over any 90 consecutive days ending in the target quarter. Since Q1 2026, a repo that crosses 1,000 stars during the quarter (or is younger than 90 days) is scored as stars at quarter end ÷ 1,000. Repos are sorted from highest to lowest score and only startup repos are kept: founded under 10 years ago, under $100M in known funding, product tied to the repo, and not acquired or public before the period ends. One repo per startup; top 20 published each quarter, top 50 in the annual report. The 2023 annual report also has a separate top-10 list by absolute stars added.

citation: Maarouf, A., Bakiaj, A., & Feuerriegel, S. (2026). Predicting Startup Success Using Large Language Models: A Novel In-Context Learning Approach. arXiv preprint arXiv:2601.16568v2 [cs.LG] (v1 23 Jan 2026; v2 27 Jan 2026). DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2601.16568. Affiliations: LMU Munich and Munich Center for Machine Learning (MCML). Preprint only; we found no journal version.
key_finding: On 4,034 early-stage Crunchbase startups, LLM in-context learning with the k most similar past startups (kNN-ICL, Gemini 2.0 Flash) reaches 0.675 to 0.713 balanced accuracy for k = 10 to 50. That beats logistic regression, random forest and XGBoost trained on the same k examples (0.537 to 0.657), a gain of about 8 percentage points at k = 50. Against ICL with randomly chosen examples it gains only about 0.2 to 1.8 points (0.713 vs 0.702 at k = 50), and a model trained on 20,172 startups still does better (0.743).
quote: Across all experiments, our kNN-ICL framework outperforms both the supervised ML baselines and vanilla ICL [...] In this case, kNN-ICL reaches a balanced accuracy of 71.3%, exceeding the supervised ML baselines (63.1%) and vanilla ICL (69.6%).
claim_note: The arXiv id exists. The authors (Maarouf, Bakiaj, Feuerriegel) and the affiliation (LMU Munich / MCML) are correct, and the paper does report that kNN-ICL beats supervised baselines when data is scarce. Caveats for a distance/kNN justification: (1) The supervised baselines are trained only on the same 10 to 50 retrieved examples for each target (p.14-15), not on the full training pool. The win is mainly LLM reasoning over a handful of examples versus ML trained on tiny n, not kNN versus well-trained supervised models. (2) Choosing examples by similarity adds little over random examples: +0.2, +0.4, +1.8 and +1.1 balanced-accuracy points at k = 10/20/30/50 (Table 7), about the size of 1 SD. (3) No pure kNN classifier without an LLM is tested. (4) A model trained on 20,172 startups scores higher (0.743 vs 0.713, Appendix Table 11). (5) Some numbers in the text do not match the tables. The intro reports baselines at 63.1% and vanilla ICL at 69.6%, while Tables 6 and 7 give 0.632/0.631/0.624 and 0.702. Page 20 says +1.7 points over vanilla ICL, but the tables give +1.1. On success, p.11 counts an IPO, an acquisition or a follow-on funding round, but p.25 says only acquisition or IPO. It is a preprint, not peer-reviewed.
metric_definition_in_paper: Data: 4,034 early-stage Crunchbase startups. Features are frozen as of end-2015: startup age, number of founders, industry, LinkedIn presence, founder gender/international/education, and a textual self-description with the company name masked. Label: success if an acquisition, IPO or follow-on funding round happens between 2016 and 2020 (35.15% positive). Retrieval: each startup is a vector of standardized structured features joined to Google embedding-001 text embeddings, with the structured part scaled to ||x_SD|| = 0.5·||x_TD||. Neighbours are ranked by cosine similarity, and the k/2 nearest successes and k/2 nearest failures are put in the prompt (k = 10/20/30/50). Prediction: Gemini 2.0 Flash, temperature 0.2. Evaluation: 5 repeated stratified 80/20 shuffle splits; balanced accuracy is the main metric.

citation: Potanin, M., Chertok, A., Zorin, K., & Shtabtsovsky, C. (2023). Startup success prediction and VC portfolio simulation using CrunchBase data. arXiv preprint arXiv:2309.15552v1 [cs.LG], 27 Sep 2023. DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2309.15552. A preprint that has not been peer reviewed. No journal version found.
key_finding: The paper trains a deep learning classifier on Crunchbase data (founder, investor, round and NMF category features) to predict whether Series B/C startups reach an IPO, an acquisition or unicorn status. It then backtests the model from 2016-01 to 2022-01, retraining every 3 months, and simulates a monthly VC portfolio: top-3 picks a month above a score threshold, a cap of about 30 companies, exit on success, write-off after 730 days without a round. The authors report a projected 14x capital growth, driven largely by the Revolut exit. Averaged over 6 yearly time-series folds, the model scores ROC AUC 0.86, precision 0.92, recall 0.64 and PR AUC 0.65.
quote: A crucial feature of our research is the simulation of fund operations based on historical data, resulting in a projected 14x capital growth of the fund’s portfolio. As per machine learning metrics, our model exhibits a robust 86% ROC_AUC.
quote_version: arXiv v1 (2309.15552v1, 27 Sep 2023; PDF dated September 28, 2023). v1 is the only version.
claim_note: The claim is accurate: the paper does predict startup success and evaluates the model with a backtested, simulated VC portfolio. Caveats for using it as a design reference: (1) It is a preprint with no peer review. (2) The 14x figure is gross: it uses only the companies that have valuation data ('Used in Capital Growth' column), sets longtime exits to 0, marks STILL_IN at last known valuation, and includes no fees or dilution. (3) Labels come from a single 2022-06-14 Crunchbase snapshot, and the 'unsuccessful' set is built with filters that depend on later information, such as no rounds since 2016 and no hiring since 2017. That is possible look-ahead in label construction, although training per window uses only companies founded, and with success known, before the window starts. (4) The main configuration is earlybird_last (enter at B/C, exit at the last success event), and the score threshold was chosen empirically.
metric_definition_in_paper: Data: Crunchbase Daily CSV Export from 2022-06-14, companies founded on or after 2000-01-01 in selected tech categories. Success = IPO (valuation >$500M or >$100M raised), acquisition (price >= max funds raised and >= $100M), or unicorn (valuation >$1B). The labeled set has 32,760 failures and 1,989 successes. Backtest from 2016-01-01 to 2022-01-01: retrain every 3 months (25 windows), and the test set is companies raising Round B/C in each window. Training uses only companies founded before the window and success events before the window. Feature functions take a date parameter to avoid leakage. Portfolio: monthly step, top-3 by score above a threshold, capacity of about 30. Exits: success (IPO/ACQ/unicorn), longtime (no round in 730 days, value 0), or STILL_IN. PnL = exit or last valuation vs entry-round valuation, split into realized and unrealized. ML metrics come from yearly time-series CV folds over 2016-2022.

citation: Cao, L., von Ehrenheim, V., Krakowski, S., Li, X., & Lutz, A. (2022/2024). Using Deep Learning to Find the Next Unicorn: A Practical Synthesis. arXiv:2210.14195 [q-fin.CP], v2 (10 Jun 2024), 49 pp. Condensed peer-reviewed version: "...A Practical Synthesis on Optimization Target, Feature Selection, Data Split and Evaluation Strategy", Proc. 5th FinNLP / 2nd Muffin Workshop at IJCAI 2023, Macao, pp. 63-73, ACL Anthology 2023.finnlp-1.6.
key_finding: This is a practical literature synthesis, not an empirical study. It reviews 29 papers and theses that predict startup success with deep learning. It groups their input features into 15 categories and finds that historical funding is the most popular one, ahead of product/service, meta information, founder and team. It also lists 13 success labels: reaching a fundraising goal, a future funding round, acquisition, IPO and others. Its recommendations are an investor-centric, time-based split with no look-ahead leakage, metrics that put precision first, and top-k portfolio simulation for evaluation. It reports no effect sizes.
quote: We identified 15 natural categories (termed funding, product/service, meta information, founder/owner, team, investor, web, context, connection, operation/planning, IP and R&D, customer, financial, M&A and data) and visualize their adoption percentage in Figure 5. [...] Historical funding is direct evidence of recognition from other early investors, thus it is the most popular category in the literature.
quote_page: 13-14 (printed page numbers; PDF pages 14-15). A footnote marker '16' after 'M&A' was omitted.
quote_version: arXiv v2 (10 Jun 2024), full extended version
claim_note: The claim is correct but too broad. The survey covers only deep-learning approaches (29 papers). It is not a survey of all startup success prediction: it treats conventional statistical and ML work only as background and points to other surveys for those. Features fall into 15 categories, with funding first. The paper also lists the success-label definitions, the evaluation metrics, and an investor-centric temporal split (Sec. 6). These are relevant to a backtest's design: avoiding look-ahead leakage and evaluating with a top-k portfolio. It reports no effect sizes. The published IJCAI-workshop version (pp. 63-73) is a condensed version of this arXiv paper.
metric_definition_in_paper: This is a survey, so it defines no single metric. The most common funding features across the reviewed papers are: total number of funding rounds and total amount raised; funding types (angel, Series A/B/C, debt); time since the latest round; size and type of the latest round; size of the seed round; per-round averages; average time between rounds; the raw time-series of rounds; and amount raised from VCs. Investor features include the number of total and distinct investors and investor reputation. Data sources are mostly Crunchbase and PitchBook. Success labels include a future funding round, acquisition, IPO, Series A, an up-round, and N-year survival, each measured over a set window after the evaluation date. The recommended split assigns each sample by its label date to a train, evaluation or test period, with features taken as snapshots using only data available up to that date.
